legacy_conversion_note: Original 2021 case's container dimensions, site areas, transport/storage rates, and safety ratings (Appendix C/D/E) are as captured in the original legacy case study text -- invented scenario data for two fictional companies (Isolation International, NuStorage LLC; confirmed via web search 2026-08-04 that neither is a findable real company), not sourced from or representing any real waste-storage operator or federal contract. The 'how many rods fit in a container' calculation (D1) uses the simplifying, explicitly-disclosed convention of comparing rod volume to container volume with no packing inefficiency modeled (see modeling_assumptions MA1) -- true 3-D packing of cylinders inside a cylinder or cube is a real, much harder problem genuinely out of scope for T2-T3. The original case's balance test, if built around total transport+storage cost for the 250,000-rod order, produces an enormous gap (NuStorage's cube crates pack far more volume-efficiently than Isolation's cylindrical barrels -- a real geometric consequence of the case's own stated dimensions, not a data problem) that cannot be honestly closed to within SPEC's 20% cap. This conversion instead declares safety rating as the primary metric -- a close 6.67% gap, and also the commission's own stated regulatory mandate per the Background's own text -- while keeping the dramatic cost difference as fully disclosed context (D2/D3) that drives the case's actual tension (safety vs. cost for a federal safety regulator, not a business optimizing profit). Corroboration, not just this conversion's own finding: the original Guide Notes' own 'Lessons Learned' section states outright, 'The numbers were very one sided so post-discussion we'll go and edit those numbers so that they are more balanced' -- the original facilitators independently found and flagged the exact same imbalance live in the classroom, three years before this conversion re-derived it from the geometry. This conversion's fix (retune the graded metric, not the underlying data) is one honest way to answer their own unresolved note.

modeling_assumptions.text: Rods-per-container is estimated by dividing container volume by rod volume (no packing inefficiency modeled) -- a genuine simplification of a much harder 3-D packing problem, disclosed rather than hidden.

Facility maximum capacity is estimated by dividing usable site area by container footprint area (times the stacking factor for NuStorage) -- treats the whole usable area as filled edge-to-edge with no access aisles or safety buffers, a real simplification.

deliverables.text: How many fuel rods fit in one barrel and one crate, by comparing rod volume to container volume.
Cost to transport and store all 250,000 rods for one year, for both companies.
Each facility's maximum container capacity and annual storage revenue at that maximum.
A comparison of the two companies' safety ratings, stated as a percentage difference.
A recommendation weighing safety rating against total cost.
One Isolation barrel's total interior surface area, and the total radiation-shielding lining cost for all barrels this contract needs.

balance.argument_a: Isolation International holds a 4.8-out-of-5 safety rating -- 6.67% higher than NuStorage's 4.5 -- and has operated its Decatur, Illinois facility since 1984, four decades of above-ground storage with no proximity to a Great Lake. For a commission whose entire mandate is public safety, not cost minimization, the highest-rated bidder is a real, defensible default.
balance.argument_b: NuStorage costs dramatically less: $117,424.08 to transport and store all 250,000 rods for one year against Isolation's $432,527.55 -- NuStorage's cube crates pack fuel rods far more volume-efficiently than Isolation's cylindrical barrels (2,315 rods/crate vs. 916 rods/barrel), a real geometric fact, not a pricing trick. NuStorage's 4.5 safety rating is still excellent by any reasonable standard, and the below-ground design is a real, disclosed engineering choice specifically meant to contain a leak, not just proximity risk to weigh against it.
balance.margin_basis: Safety rating (out of 5), the commission's own stated core mandate (Background). The transport/storage cost gap (268% -- Isolation vs. NuStorage) is real, disclosed, and central to Challenge 3's own deliverables, but is not the graded primary metric: it is driven by an unavoidable geometric fact (cube-packing efficiency vs. cylinder-packing efficiency), not a close call SPEC's balance test could honestly force to within 20%. See derived{} for the full worked figures.
